You use reported speech (indirect speech) when you are saying (reporting) what other people said.
When writing, it is common to use reported speech in storytelling and narrations. It allows the writer to share dialogue with the reader without always using quotation marks.

When you tell people what someone has said you generally make the verb tense 'more in the past' since we are reporting the information at a later time. You need to change the verb to the next past form.

You have to change the pronoun if you are reporting what someone else said. Compare these two sentences. In each case the person actually said "I don't want to go."
• I said, “I don't want to go.” > I said I didn't want to go.
• Bill said, “I don't want to go.” > Bill said he didn't want to go.

Direct: Sally told me “I kissed all the boys when I was in school”.
Indirect: Sally told me that she had kissed all the boys when she had been in school.

When you want to report questions asked, the subject normally comes before the verb.
When the question is a yes/no questions, you use if or whether to report it.
He asked if/whether we could talk.
Look at the chart below to see the changes in verb tense.

You use tag questions to ask for clarification and confirmation.
Question tags are short questions at the end of statements.
They are mainly used in speech when we want to:
• confirm that something is true or not, or
• to encourage a reply from the person we are speaking to.

1. A positive statement is followed by a negative question tag. Use this when you think the other person will agree by saying ‘yes'
    • You were taken by surprise, weren't you?
    • You are Canadian, aren't you?
    • She has a brother, doesn't she?
    • He can speak English, can't he?

1. A negative statement is followed by a positive question tag. Use this when you think the other person will agree by saying ‘no'
    • You weren't taken by surprise, were you?
    • You aren't Canadian, are you?
    • She doesn't have a brother, does she?
    • He can't speak English, can he?

If the main verb is to be or a modal verb, the tag will be the same.
For all other main verbs, use the tag do/does or did/didn't. Look at the examples in the chart.

images.text:
Peter: Sally you're a popular girl, aren't you?
Sally: You know it.
Peter: You were popular in school, weren't you?
Sally: Pretty popular.
Peter: So tell me, who was your best friend in elementary school?
Sally: Oh wow! That's a difficult question, isn't it? So long ago. I would say my best friend was Michelle Reynolds. We grew up together and used to always play together after school. We were thick as thieves. She was fun and a little bit naughty too. She would always start rumors and spread gossip. One day she told a boy that I liked that I liked him. The next day he came up to me and told me what Michelle said. He asked me if I wanted a kiss.

Peter: What did you say?
Sally: I said Gross! punched him in the arm and ran away. I didn't like him after that and he never asked again.
Peter: You were mad at Michelle, weren't you?
Sally: Not really, but I got her back. I told a boy she liked that she had cooties.
Peter: Cooties? That means germs, doesn't it?
Sally: Yep. Classic but effective.

Vanessa: Hey guys. What are you talking about?
Peter: Sally told me that she kissed all the boys when she was in school.
Sally: Peter!
Peter: She also said she liked to spread rumors and gossip.
Sally: I'm going to give you such a smack.
Peter: She told me she kissed a boy once and he said, “oh, gross”.
Sally: You are such a jerk! He is such a jerk, isn't he?
Vanessa: He is a bad man.
